title: The feasts, looking back
hookLine: a year that turns and turns
tomorrow: a father says 'I believe' and 'help my unbelief' at once. why?

cards: Some neighbors put up Christmas lights in November, and some neighbors grumble. Inside churches there's an older, friendlier argument.

Purple cloth on the altar, then white, then purple again, red, and a long run of green: in some churches you can tell the season by the colors. In others the walls never change, and every Sunday is the feast.
So which is it: the turning year, or the plain Sunday?

teach.b: One side keeps the whole circle. Advent waits in the dark. Christmas, the birth.
Lent, a season of turning that remembers Jesus in the desert. Holy Week, Easter, then Pentecost's wind and fire, and the long green stretch some churches call Ordinary Time.
Ecclesiastes gives them their line: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.” The same stories come round, and the person hearing them has changed.
Christmas in a hard year isn't the Christmas of childhood.
The other side keeps Sunday at the center. Every first day of the week is resurrection day, they say, the day the tomb was found empty.
Paul writes about one person who esteems one day above another, and another who esteems every day alike, and says: “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.”
For them, a crowded calendar risks letting a few big days outshine the ordinary week, where faith is lived. Each side guards something.
One guards the story told in order, so nothing gets skipped. The other guards the plain Sunday, so no week goes uncelebrated.
And both can stand on the same psalm: “This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.”

how: Churches that follow a church year change their readings, music and sometimes their colors through Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter and Pentecost; others keep Sunday as the main feast of every week.

games.q: the turning year — tap the pairs.

s: every church keeps the same full calendar of feasts
some keep the whole year; others keep Sunday as the main feast.
'Ordinary Time' means the dull, unimportant part of the year
it's the long green stretch between the big seasons, weeks where growing happens quietly.
Paul tells people who keep days differently to be fully persuaded in their own minds

games.q: your cousin's church keeps no seasons, just Sundays. you love Advent. what's the best case for her side?
o: seasons came later in church history, so they don't count.
a plain Sunday keeps Easter every week, so no ordinary week is skipped.
her church just hasn't learned about the calendar yet.
games.why: the Sunday side guards the ordinary week: every first day is resurrection day. the seasons side guards the story told in order. both meet in Psalm 118:24.

practice: Open a calendar, on your phone or the wall, and find today. Ask two questions: in the church year, what season might this be, and in this plain week, what makes today worth keeping?
If you pray, rest on the psalm: this is the day which the LORD hath made.

wordCard.voice: The feasts. A church year that walks through the life of Jesus, and a Sunday that comes round every single week.

orig.note: Greek: Pascha, a name for Easter used by Orthodox Christians and others. 1 Corinthians 5:7 uses it: Christ our passover.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the circle turns, and the one hearing the story is a little different each time round. Day seventeen-seventy-four, in its season.
